Answers below, all verified against the source.

## 1. `deleteComment` — no, it does not check who wrote the comment

`ArticleService.deleteComment` (`src/article/article.service.ts:114`) takes only `(slug, id)`:

```ts
async deleteComment(slug: string, id: string): Promise<ArticleRO> {
  let article = await this.articleRepository.findOne({slug});
  const comment = await this.commentRepository.findOne(id);
  const deleteIndex = article.comments.findIndex(_comment => _comment.id === comment.id);
  ...
```

The only thing it verifies is that the comment actually belongs to that article (the `findIndex` on `article.comments`); if it doesn't, it silently returns the article unchanged rather than erroring.

The caller doesn't help either — `ArticleController.deleteComment` (`src/article/article.controller.ts:85`) is `async deleteComment(@Param() params)`. There's no `@User('id')` parameter at all, so the caller's identity never reaches the service.

And there is nothing to compare against even if you wanted to: `Comment` (`src/article/comment.entity.ts`) has only `id`, `body`, and a `ManyToOne` back to `article` — **no author column**, and `addComment` only sets `comment.body`. So comment ownership isn't recorded anywhere.

Net effect: `DELETE /articles/:slug/comments/:id` is behind `AuthMiddleware` (`src/article/article.module.ts:29`), so you need a valid token — but *any* authenticated user can delete *any* comment. The `@ApiResponse({ status: 403 })` on the handler is aspirational; nothing returns 403.

Side note: if `:id` doesn't match any comment row, `comment` is `undefined` and `comment.id` on line 118 throws a TypeError → 500.

## 2. Profile routes with `AuthMiddleware`

From `src/profile/profile.module.ts:19-23`, the middleware is applied to exactly one path, for `RequestMethod.ALL`:

| Route | Guarded? |
|---|---|
| `POST /profiles/:username/follow` | ✅ yes |
| `DELETE /profiles/:username/follow` | ✅ yes (same path, `ALL` covers it) |
| `GET /profiles/:username` | ❌ no |

`getProfile` is public. It still takes `@User('id') userId`, which works because the `@User` decorator (`src/user/user.decorator.ts:13`) falls back to decoding the token itself when the middleware hasn't run — so an anonymous call gets `userId === undefined` and the profile is returned without `following` resolved, rather than a 401.

## 3. The `RO` suffix = "Response Object"

It marks the outer envelope type that gets serialized to the HTTP response body, as opposed to the `*Data` / `*Entity` types that describe the resource itself. Every `RO` interface is a single-key wrapper matching the RealWorld API spec's JSON shape:

```ts
export interface ArticleRO  { article: ArticleEntity; }                        // article.interface.ts:24
export interface ArticlesRO { articles: ArticleEntity[]; articlesCount: number; }
export interface CommentsRO { comments: Comment[]; }
export interface ProfileRO  { profile: ProfileData; }                          // profile.interface.ts:8
export interface UserRO     { user: UserData; }                                // user.interface.ts:9
```

That's why the services all `return {article}` / `return {articles, articlesCount}` — the wrapping is the whole point, so the client receives `{"article": {...}}` rather than a bare object. The convention pairs with the un-suffixed `ArticleData` / `ProfileData` / `UserData` interfaces, which describe the payload *inside* the envelope. (Note `ArticleRO` actually wraps `ArticleEntity`, not `ArticleData` — `ArticleData` is declared but unused in that file.)
